'''''Campanula rapunculoides''''', known by the common names '''creeping bellflower''', '''rampion bellflower''', rover bellflower, garden bluebell, creeping bluebell, purple bell, garden harebell, and creeping campanula,<ref name="Calgary">{{citation |url=http://www.calgary.ca/CSPS/Parks/Pages/Planning-and-Operations/Pest-Management/Garden-centres-free-of-invasive-plants.aspx |title=Garden centres free of invasive plants |accessdate=5 August 2015 |work=City of Calgary Parks Department |location=[[Calgary, Alberta]] |date=nd |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120602175655/http://www.calgary.ca/CSPS/Parks/Pages/Planning-and-Operations/Pest-Management/Garden-centres-free-of-invasive-plants.aspx |archive-date=2012-06-02 |url-status=dead }}</ref> is a [[perennial]] [[herbaceous]] plant of the genus ''[[Campanula]]'', belonging to the family [[Campanulaceae]]. Native to central and southern Europe and west Asia,<ref name=bentham>[https://books.google.com/books?id=QH9IAAAAYAAJ&dq=Campanula+rapunculoides&pg=PA513 Handbook of the British flora: a description of ..., Volume 2; Volume 1865 By George Bentham]</ref> in some parts of North America it is an extremely [[invasive species]].<ref name="Dyer">{{cite web |last1=Dyer |first1=Mary H. |title=Creeping Bellflower - How To Get Rid Of Creeping Bellflower |url=https://www.gardeningknowhow.com/ornamental/flowers/campanula/removing-creeping-bellflower.htm |website=gardeningknownhow.com |access-date=12 June 2021}}</ref>

==Etymology==
The genus Latin name (''Campanula''), meaning  'small bell', refers to the bell-shape of the flower, while the specific name (''rapunculoides'') refers to the similarity to ''[[Campanula rapunculus]]''.

==Description==
[[File:Campanulaceae - Campanula rapunculoides-4.JPG|thumb|240px|left|Close-up on flowers of ''Campanula rapunculoides'']] ''Campanula rapunculoides'' reaches on average {{convert|30|-|80|cm}} of height, with a maximum of {{convert|120|cm}}.  The stem is simple, erect and lightly [[pubescent (botany)|pubescent]] and the leaves are usually shortly hairy. The [[basal leaves]] are triangular, narrow, with a heart-shaped or rounded base, jagged edges and are up to {{convert|12|cm}} long.  The upper stem leaves are [[sessility (botany)|sessile]], lanceolate, and shortly stalked.

The [[inflorescence]] consists of  nodding spikelike [[racemes]] with numerous drooping flowers. The flowers are bright blue-violet (rarely white), {{convert|2|to|4|cm|in}} long, with short [[Petiole (botany)|petioles]] standing to one side in the [[axils]] of the [[bracts]]. The bracts are quite different and smaller than the leaves. The [[sepals]] are lanceolate to ovate-lanceolate, entire, wide at the base up to {{convert|2.5|mm}}. The [[Corolla (botany)|corolla]] is bell-shaped, with five deep lobes slightly [[Glossary of leaf morphology#Edge|ciliate]]. The flowering period extends from June through September. The flowers are pollinated by insects (bees, flies, butterflies, etc.) ([[entomophily]]). The fruit is a capsule with five pores near the base, where the seeds are spread.

The plant seeds abundantly (each plant can produce 15,000 seeds),<ref>{{citation |url=https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/creeping-bellflower |title=Campanula rapunculoides (Creeping Bellflower) |series=Minnesota Wild flowers |work= Minnesota Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund |accessdate=5 August 2015 |date=nd |location=[[Minnesota]]}}</ref> and while some roots come out when it is pulled, the horizontal rhizomes grow vertical storage tubers, which may not be anywhere near the surface portions of the plant. These storage tubers can regrow rhizomes, which in turn send up shoots at some distance from the storage tubers.<ref name="umich">{{cite web |last1=Stannard |first1=Katie |title=Invasive of the Week: Creeping bellflower (Campanula rapunculoides)|institution=Matthaei Botanical Gardens and Nichols Arboretum, University of Michigan |url=https://mbgna.umich.edu/invasive-of-the-week-creeping-bellflower-campanula-rapunculoides/ |date=28 May 2020}}</ref> 
 
This plant has its overwintering buds situated just below the soil surface ([[Raunkiær plant life-form#Hemicryptophytes|hemicryptophyte]]). It spreads by underground [[rhizome]]s and produces deep, [[taproot]]-shaped [[tuber]]s. Both are white and fleshy. Because any piece of the roots can sprout into a new plant, it is extremely hard to eradicate.

==Distribution==
This plant is native to Europe and western Siberia,<ref name="umich"/> where it grows in semi-shaded areas like open woods, the edges of denser forests, and meadowland.<ref name=bentham/> It has been introduced to North America, where it has become an extremely invasive weed;<ref name="masterg"/> it chokes out other plants, and eliminating it is nearly impossible due to its multiple propagation mechanisms.<ref name="umich"/>

Like many related ''[[Campanula]]'' species and more distant relatives,<ref name=gfw>{{cite web |title=Campanula: Edible Bellflowers – GoodFood World |url=https://www.goodfoodworld.com/2014/04/campanula-edible-bellflowers/https://www.goodfoodworld.com/2014/04/campanula-edible-bellflowers/}}</ref> it is edible and was historically grown for food. The roots, shoots, and leaves are all edible.<ref name="masterg">{{cite web |title=Creeping Bellflower |url=https://mastergardener.extension.wisc.edu/files/2015/12/Campanula_rapunculoides.pdf |website=Wisconsin Master Gardener |publisher=University of Wisconsin-Madison |date=6 July 2009}}</ref> The roots can be eaten raw or cooked, and the upper parts are mild-flavoured;<ref name="NPT">{{cite web |title=Campanula rapunculoides (creeping bellflower): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/campanula/rapunculoides/ |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org |publisher=[[Native Plant Trust]]}}</ref> indeed rather bland,<ref name=gfw/> commonplace, and somewhat chewy-leaved; the basal leaves are often cooked as a [[pot herb]], where they blend in with other leaves unnoticeably.<ref>{{cite web |title=Creeping Bellflower |url=https://foragerchef.com/creeping-bellflower/ |website=FORAGER CHEF |date=8 April 2020}}</ref>

==Habitat==
It grows  on grassy places, dry hills, meadows, in deciduous and pine forests, woods, fields and roadsides, along railway lines and hedgerows, preferably in partial shade, in dry to moist sites and on clay soils, relatively rich in nitrogen, at an altitude of {{convert|0|-|2000|m}} above sea level. It also occurs in cultivated fields as a weed.

==Invasive species==

''Campanula rapunculoides'' is native to parts of Eurasia, but is a widespread European import to North America, and it is invasive.<ref>{{citation |url=https://www.minnesotawildflowers.info/flower/creeping-bellflower |title=Campanula rapunculoides (Creeping Bellflower) |series=Minnesota Wild flowers |work= Minnesota Environment and Natural Resources Trust Fund |accessdate=5 August 2015 |date=nd |location=[[Minnesota]]}}</ref>

It is extremely difficult to remove.<ref name="umich"/> Mechanical removal, burning, and chemicals have varying success rates, but there is no sure method of removing the plants first try.<ref>{{cite web |first1=Brendon |last1=Panke |first2=Ryan |last2=deRegnier |first3=Mark |last3=Renz |title=Management of invasive plants in Wisconsin: Creeping bellflower (A3924-05) |url=https://douglas.extension.wisc.edu/files/2015/07/Creeping-Bellflower.pdf |publisher=University of Wisconsin-Extension, Cooperative Extension}}</ref>
